mainTopic: Whether an unclear vow expression (יָדַיִם שֶׁאֵין מוֹכִיחוֹת) counts. אביי and רבא are tested against two ברייתות and linked to the מחלוקת of רבי יהודה and the רבנן.
overview: This amud continues the dispute between אביי and רבא about an unclear 'handle' to a vow (יד שאינה מוכיחה). אביי says it works, and רבא says it does not. It opens with the end of רבא's claim that his view fits even the רבנן: their leniency with a גט proves nothing for other cases. Next, a ברייתא seems to refute אביי, since 'הרי הוא עלי' forbids the object, implying that without 'עלי' it does not. אביי's first answer, that he may have meant הפקר or צדקה, is pushed back. So the ברייתא is reread: without 'עלי' the object is forbidden to everyone, because he may have meant הקדש. A second ברייתא, about 'this is a חטאת' versus 'this is my חטאת', is answered by saying it follows רבי יהודה. אביי then retracts his earlier claim that his view fits רבי יהודה too. Finally, רבא shows that his own view still fits the רבנן, because they are lenient only with a גט, where a man cannot divorce someone else's wife.

steps.title: The divorce case proves nothing about unclear expressions in general
steps.stepSummary: רבא's side finishes rejecting the proof from a גט. There the meaning is clear only because a man cannot divorce someone else's wife. That does not show that unclear expressions work everywhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: …since a man does not divorce his friend's wife. But in general, did you ever hear them say that unclear expressions work?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a rejection that began on the previous amud. There, the גמרא tried to tie אביי to the רבנן (who are lenient about a גט) and רבא to רבי יהודה. Here רבא's side answers that the רבנן's leniency about a גט does not prove anything for other cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a גט, the husband's partial wording is obviously about his own wife, because nobody can divorce another man's wife. So that case is really a clear expression, not an unclear one. It cannot prove that unclear expressions (ידים שאין מוכיחות) count in general.

keyTerms.term: אֵין אָדָם מְגָרֵשׁ אֶת אֵשֶׁת חֲבֵירוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: A man cannot divorce another man's wife
Did you ever hear them say so?

steps.confusionAlert: This line begins in the middle of a sentence. The case it refers to (a גט with partial wording) was discussed just before this passage.

phrases.english: since a man does not divorce
did you hear them say it?
phrases.notes: He means: did the חכמים ever say that unclear wording works in ordinary cases?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the rejection of the proof from גט that began before this passage.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the גט case as proof for אביי.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The גט case is clear from its context, so it is not a true example of an unclear expression.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to refute אביי
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that "הרי הוא עלי" forbids the object. The inference is that without "עלי" it is not forbidden, which seems to show that unclear expressions do not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: If someone says "It is upon me" or "This is upon me," the object is forbidden, because it is a handle to a קרבן. The reason is that he said "upon me"; if he did not say "upon me," it is not forbidden. This refutes אביי!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to attack אביי's view that unclear expressions count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא stresses the word "עלי." Saying only "הרי הוא" is unclear, because we cannot tell what he means. If that is not forbidden, then an unclear expression does not work, which is exactly רבא's view.

keyTerms.meaning: It is hereby upon me (forbidden to me)
A 'handle' (partial expression) pointing to a קרבן-style vow
The reason is that… (this sets up an inference from the opposite case)

phrases.english: "This is upon me" — it is forbidden,
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: because it is a handle to a קרבן.
The reason is that he said "upon me"
but if he did not say "upon me" — no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof for אביי is rejected, a challenge against him comes next.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's view that ידים שאין מוכיחות count as ידים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא requires "עלי." This implies that the unclear "הרי הוא" alone does nothing.

steps.title: אביי: without "עלי" he may have meant הפקר or צדקה
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that "הרי הוא" without "עלי" is not an unclear vow at all. It could mean "it is הפקר" or "it is צדקה."
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי can tell you: the reason it is forbidden is that he said "upon me." But if he said "It is…" without "upon me," he may be saying "It is ownerless" or "It is charity."
steps.whatsHappening: אביי defends himself by explaining why "הרי הוא" alone does not forbid the object.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי says the issue is not that unclear expressions fail. "הרי הוא" alone may not point to a vow at all, because it could be about הפקר or צדקה. So it is not a 'handle' to a vow in the first place, and his rule is not touched.

keyTerms.meaning: He can say to you (he would answer)

phrases.english: The reason is that he said "upon me"
or "It is charity" is what he is saying.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: without "עלי" the words are not a vow handle at all.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's inference means unclear vow handles fail.
steps.terutzMaskana: Without "עלי" the words may be about הפקר or צדקה, so they do not point to a vow.

steps.title: But the ברייתא's reason is about a קרבן handle
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges אביי's answer. The ברייתא gives its reason as "יד לקרבן," so the discussion is about the strength of a vow handle, not about הפקר or צדקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the ברייתא teaches "because it is a handle to a קרבן"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on אביי's answer from step 3.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא frames the whole case in terms of a handle to a קרבן. So the difference between saying "עלי" and not saying it must be about whether the handle is clear enough. That brings back the original problem for אביי.

phrases.english: a handle to a קרבן" that it teaches!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהוּא יָד לְקׇרְבָּן קָתָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's reading that "הרי הוא" means הפקר or צדקה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's stated reason is about a קרבן handle, so the alternative meanings do not fit its framing.

steps.title: Reread the ברייתא: without "עלי" both people are forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is reread. With "עלי," only the speaker is forbidden. Without "עלי," everyone is forbidden, because he may have meant הקדש. The ברייתא no longer refutes אביי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: the reason is that he said "upon me," so he is forbidden and his friend is permitted. But if he said only "It is…," both are forbidden, since perhaps he is saying "It is consecrated."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer for אביי by changing what the inference from "עלי" means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The opposite case is no longer read as "not forbidden." It is read as "even more forbidden." "עלי" limits the prohibition to the speaker. Without it, he may have declared the object הקדש, which forbids it to everyone. So the ברייתא does not say that unclear expressions fail.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say (reread the source this way)

steps.whatToRemember: Without "עלי," the object is not permitted. It is forbidden to everyone, because the speaker may have made it הקדש. So the ברייתא no longer refutes אביי.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read "without עלי" as "less forbidden." In this answer it is MORE forbidden: the friend is forbidden too.

phrases.english: The reason is that he said "upon me"
he is forbidden and his friend is permitted,
since perhaps he is saying "It is consecrated."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of step 3 with a new reading of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereads the inference: the opposite case is stricter, not more lenient.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without "עלי" the object is permitted, because the unclear handle fails.
steps.terutzMaskana: Without "עלי" both people are forbidden, because of a possible הקדש. So the ברייתא does not refute אביי.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that adding "עלי" narrows a declaration to a personal vow. Without it, the words could be a full הקדש.

steps.title: A ברייתא about sin-offerings seems to refute אביי
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says 'this is a חטאת' accomplishes nothing, while 'this is my חטאת' works. Since an unclear expression fails, this seems to refute אביי.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: If someone says 'This is a חטאת' or 'This is an אשם', he has said nothing, even though he owes a חטאת and an אשם. If he says 'This is my חטאת' or 'This is my אשם', and he did owe one, his words take effect. This is a refutation of אביי!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that seems to prove unclear expressions do not work, against אביי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without 'my', the words do not clearly tie the animal to his own obligation, so they are an unclear expression. The ברייתא says such words do nothing, even when he really owes the offering. Adding 'my' makes the words clear, and then they work. This goes straight against אביי, who says unclear expressions do work.

keyTerms.meaning: He has said nothing (his words have no effect)

phrases.english: "This is a sin-offering," "This is a guilt-offering,"
phrases.notes: He is pointing at an animal, but he does not say whose offering it is.

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא חַיָּיב חַטָּאת וְאָשָׁם
phrases.english: even though he is obligated to bring a sin-offering and a guilt-offering
"This is my sin-offering," "This is my guilt-offering,"
This is a refutation of Abaye!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The earlier ברייתא was reread so it no longer refuted אביי. Now the גמרא brings a different ברייתא against him.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's view that unclear expressions work
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'This is a חטאת' is an unclear expression and the ברייתא says it does nothing. So unclear expressions do not work.

steps.title: אביי says the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that this ברייתא follows רבי יהודה, who does not accept unclear expressions. The רבנן disagree with him, and אביי holds like the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי could say to you: Whose view is this ברייתא? It is רבי יהודה's.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי escapes the refutation by saying the ברייתא follows only one תנא, רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי does not argue with how the ברייתא reads. He says it follows רבי יהודה, who is strict about unclear expressions. So it is no refutation of אביי if he holds like the רבנן, who argue with רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: He could say to you (a defense on his behalf)

steps.confusionAlert: On the previous amud (5b), אביי claimed his view works even for רבי יהודה. That is exactly why the next step attacks this answer.

phrases.notes: רבי יהודה is the one who says a גט's wording has to be fully clear.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ אַבָּיֵי הָא מַנִּי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִיא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the source to one side of a מחלוקת (אוקימתא by תנא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא is a universal rule against unclear expressions.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא follows only רבי יהודה, and אביי follows the רבנן.

steps.title: But אביי said his view fits even רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that אביי himself said earlier that his view fits even רבי יהודה, so he cannot push the ברייתא off onto רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But wasn't it אביי himself who said: What I said holds even according to רבי יהודה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges אביי's answer by pointing out that it contradicts his own earlier statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If אביי's view works even for רבי יהודה, then a ברייתא following רבי יהודה should still fit אביי. But it does not fit him. So saying 'it is רבי יהודה' does not save him.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it so that (introduces a contradiction)

phrases.english: But wasn't it Abaye who said:
is even according to Rabbi Yehuda!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אַבָּיֵי הוּא דְּאָמַר אֲנָא דַּאֲמַרִי אֲפִילּוּ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's answer that the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: אביי earlier said his view fits even רבי יהודה. So a ברייתא that follows רבי יהודה should still fit him, yet it clearly does not.

steps.title: אביי took back his earlier claim
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that אביי retracted. He now admits that רבי יהודה does not accept unclear expressions, and his own view follows only the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: In two words, the גמרא answers that אביי changed his mind about his earlier claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because of this ברייתא, אביי no longer says his view fits רבי יהודה. Now the question of unclear expressions depends on the מחלוקת between רבי יהודה and the רבנן, and אביי sides with the רבנן.
steps.whatToRemember: After this step, אביי's view that unclear expressions work follows only the רבנן, not רבי יהודה.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in step 8.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אביי's view fits both רבי יהודה and the רבנן.
steps.terutzMaskana: אביי's view fits only the רבנן. רבי יהודה rejects unclear expressions.

steps.title: Does רבא now follow only רבי יהודה?
steps.stepSummary: Since the רבנן seem to accept unclear expressions, the גמרא asks whether רבא, who rejects them, must hold like רבי יהודה alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: But shall we say that רבא holds like רבי יהודה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to רבא and asks whether his view now has to be limited to רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי just gave up his claim that his view fits רבי יהודה. So the גמרא asks whether רבא must likewise give up his claim that his view fits the רבנן. If he did, his view would follow only רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: that Rava holds in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לֵימָא רָבָא דְּאָמַר כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 9's conclusion that the topic depends on the רבי יהודה and רבנן מחלוקת, and applies it to רבא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's view that unclear expressions do not work
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the רבנן accept unclear expressions, then רבא's view is left following only רבי יהודה, the minority.

steps.title: רבא: the רבנן are lenient only with a גט
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that his view fits even the רבנן. They do not require clear wording only for a גט, since a man cannot divorce someone else's wife. Everywhere else, they too require clear wording.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא could say to you: What I said holds even according to the רבנן. The רבנן only said that clear wording is not needed in the case of a גט, because a man cannot divorce his friend's wife. But in general, clear wording is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends himself by limiting the רבנן's leniency to a גט alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a גט, the context already makes the meaning clear: it can only be for his own wife. So the רבנן's leniency there is not really about accepting unclear expressions. In other cases, such as vows, no such context exists, so even the רבנן require clear wording, which fits רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: Clear expressions that show the meaning

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides can now fit the רבנן. אביי says they accept unclear expressions. רבא says they are lenient only with a גט, where the meaning is clear anyway.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the same reasoning as step 1, used here to show that רבא is not stuck holding a minority view.

phrases.english: What I said is even according to the Rabbis.
that we do not require clear expressions
only regarding a bill of divorce,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאֵין אָדָם מְגָרֵשׁ אֶת אֵשֶׁת חֲבֵירוֹ.
phrases.english: since a person cannot divorce his friend's wife.
But in general, we require clear expressions.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ רָבָא אֲנָא דַּאֲמַרִי אֲפִילּוּ לְרַבָּנַן
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the רבנן's ruling to a special case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רבנן accept unclear expressions everywhere, so רבא follows only רבי יהודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן are lenient only with a גט, where the context makes the meaning clear. Elsewhere they require clear wording, so רבא fits the רבנן.
